real_title: R (on the application of Bano) v London Borough of Waltham Forest
anonymised_title: R (on the application of the Appellant) v A London Borough Council (local housing authority)
appeal_from: Court of Appeal (Civil Division), [2025] EWCA Civ 92; [2025] 1 WLR 2557 (Peter Jackson, Newey and Warby LJJ), reversing the High Court, [2024] EWHC 654 (Admin) (Deputy High Court Judge)
facts: In January 2017 the Appellant, a single parent of two children, applied to a local housing authority as a homeless person under Part 7 of the Housing Act 1996. By letter of 23 February 2017 the authority accepted that it owed her the main housing duty under section 193(2). She and her children were placed in temporary accommodation in another London borough. On 11 June 2020 the authority emailed her a letter (the Offer Letter) offering an assured shorthold tenancy of a flat in a city outside London for a fixed term of 24 months. The letter stated that the offer would discharge the authority's duty whether she accepted or refused it, that it was a one-off offer, that she could request a review of the suitability of the accommodation within 21 days, and that failure to attend a viewing on 15 June would be treated as refusal. It informed her of the effect of section 195A(1) but not section 195A(2). Her daughter replied that the family could not move and asked to be relocated locally. The authority responded that its duty was discharged whether or not she accepted, and cancelled the temporary accommodation. It is common ground that the Appellant refused the offer. No review was requested within 21 days (expiring 2 July 2020). Later letters from the authority (7 October 2020, 30 May 2023) treated review requests as out of time and affirmed that the duty had ended. The authority accepts that, had a review been sought in time, the omission concerning section 195A(2) would have led to the review succeeding. She was evicted from the temporary accommodation under a possession order in March 2024 and was later granted a tenancy by the authority; the appeal is academic as regards her but was heard in the public interest. In August 2023 she issued judicial review proceedings challenging the authority's refusal to accept that the main housing duty continued. The authority said she had an alternative remedy, a section 202 review and section 204 appeal. The Deputy High Court Judge held that the duty had not ended because the authority had made and notified no decision that the offer was accepted or refused, so no review right arose. The Court of Appeal allowed the authority's appeal, holding that the duty ceased automatically on refusal, that the Offer Letter or a later confirmatory decision was reviewable, and that a section 202 review was a suitable alternative remedy. The Appellant appeals to the Supreme Court.

issues.question: On the proper construction of section 193(7AA) of the Housing Act 1996, does the main housing duty cease automatically when the applicant accepts or refuses a compliant private rented sector offer, without the authority having to make and notify a further decision that the offer was accepted or refused?
Was the Offer Letter itself a decision of the authority that was capable of being the subject of a request for review under section 202(1) of the Housing Act 1996?

Did the authority's communications after the Offer Letter, to the extent they merely affirmed that the main housing duty had ended, constitute decisions giving rise to a fresh right to request a review under section 202(1)?

appellant_submissions: Section 193(7AA) should be read as requiring the authority to decide whether the applicant has accepted or refused the offer, and to notify that decision, before the duty ends. The separate limbs (a) accepts and (b) refuses suggest the authority must determine which applies, and there may be genuine debate about that. The offer must warn of the 'possible' consequence of refusal or acceptance, which indicates that a later notified decision is needed to confirm those consequences have occurred. Section 202 presupposes a decision that is notified to the applicant, because the 21-day period under section 202(3) runs from notification; without a decision there is no review right and so no alternative remedy that bars judicial review. The Offer Letter was at most a statement of intention or prospective decision. Warsame and Ravichandran proceed on the footing that the authority makes a reviewable decision. An automatic-cessation construction produces unworkable or impracticable results: short deadlines and treating non-attendance at a viewing as refusal; applicants unaware that the duty has ended (for example a change of eligibility); and offer letters that go astray. The common law requires an adverse decision to be communicated before it binds the person affected (Anufrijeva). The intervener Shelter supported these points and referred to evidence that most authorities send a separate discharge letter. The Appellant also contended that the post-offer letters could not found a review right.
respondent_submissions: Section 193(7AA) says the authority 'shall also cease to be subject to the duty' if the applicant accepts or refuses a compliant offer. It does not refer to the authority deciding, being satisfied or notifying, and the Appellant's reading would insert extra words. Section 193(5)(c) expressly requires notification, which shows Parliament knew how to require it where intended. The legislative history of section 193(7), under which post-refusal satisfaction and notification requirements were removed, supports automatic cessation. The word 'possible' is explained by the possibility of a successful challenge to suitability. The Offer Letter, which must be given in writing, is itself the authority's decision that the duty will end on acceptance or refusal, it is notified to the applicant, and the 21-day period runs from it, so section 202 operates coherently. The authority has discretion to extend time under section 202(3). Extreme cases of unreasonably short deadlines can be challenged on review, and an applicant can accept and then seek review. The Appellant's construction is itself absurd because the duty would continue indefinitely, even for a tenant who has moved in, if the authority omitted to decide and notify. A review under sections 202 and 204 is the suitable alternative remedy that Parliament provided, judicial review being a remedy of last resort. Allowing review of later confirmatory letters would circumvent the 21-day limit. The Fourteen London boroughs and the Social Housing Law Association intervened in support.
legal_materials: Housing Act 1996 s193(2): the authority 'shall secure that accommodation is available for occupation by the applicant'. s193(3): the authority is subject to the duty 'until it ceases by virtue of any of the following provisions'. s193(5)(c): duty ceases where, inter alia, 'the authority notify the applicant that they regard themselves as ceasing to be subject to the duty'. s193(7AA): 'The authority shall also cease to be subject to the duty under this section if the applicant, having been informed in writing of the matters mentioned in subsection (7AB)- (a) accepts a private rented sector offer, or (b) refuses such an offer.' s193(7AB): possible consequence of refusal or acceptance; right to request review of suitability; effect of s195A. s202(1)(b), (g), (1A): right to request review of decisions on what duty is owed and on suitability of a private rented sector offer. s202(3): request within 21 days of notification of the decision or such longer period as the authority may in writing allow. s204: county court appeal on a point of law. Authorities: Warsame v Hounslow LBC [2000] 1 WLR 696; Ravichandran v Lewisham LBC [2010] EWCA Civ 755; Norton v Haringey LBC [2022] EWCA Civ 1340; R (Glencore) v HMRC [2017] EWCA Civ 1716; In re McAleenon [2024] UKSC 31; R (Anufrijeva) v SSHD [2003] UKHL 36.
actual_reasoning_summary: The Court held that on its plain words section 193(7AA) ends the main housing duty by operation of law when the applicant accepts or refuses a compliant offer; no further authority decision or notification is required. This was supported by the contrast with section 193(5)(c), by the amendment history of section 193(7), and by the absurdity of the contrary reading. Section 202 still works, because the Offer Letter is itself the notified, reviewable decision that the duty will end on acceptance or refusal, with the 21 days running from the letter and time extendable under section 202(3). The Court rejected the absurdity and procedural fairness arguments, noting a letter not received would mean no acceptance or refusal and the duty would continue. It disagreed with the Court of Appeal that purely confirmatory later letters are reviewable, since that would circumvent the 21-day limit and the discretion to extend time; the error did not affect the outcome. The Appellant had a suitable alternative remedy by way of section 202 review, which precluded judicial review.
outcome_evidence: Para 111: "Mrs Bano had a suitable alternative remedy by way of review under section 202 which precludes her claim for judicial review. We would dismiss the appeal." See also para 97: "We would dismiss this ground of appeal." and para 102 (grounds 1 and 2 dispose of the appeal). Lord Reed, Lord Sales and Lord Hamblen agree with Lord Stephens and Lady Rose (para 6 header).
